Findings.Comment: `totalWithVat` converts the `Cents` subtotal to floating-point euros (`subtotal(lines) / 100`), multiplies by `(1 + vatRate)`, then scales back with `* 100`. This is exactly the floating-point euro arithmetic the project bans: for `subtotal = 100` cents and `vatRate = 0.2`, `1 * 1.2` is `1.2000000000000002` in IEEE-754, so the returned value is `120.00000000000003`, a `Cents` amount that is not an integer and cannot be compared, summed or displayed reliably. Every non-trivial subtotal/vatRate pair produces rounding drift instead of whole cents.
Findings.Headline: totalWithVat does VAT math in floating-point euros
Evidence: export function totalWithVat(lines: Line[], vatRate: number): Cents {

Expected.why: The total is computed in floating-point euros and returned unrounded as Cents, which the blocking rule forbids and which yields fractional cents.

Findings.Comment: This new log line writes `c.Email` and `c.IBAN` to the application log on every successful create. Email and IBAN are exactly the customer personal data the project's blocking guideline forbids logging, so a single successful `POST /customers` request places both into the log stream, which is typically shipped to a log aggregator with broader access than the customer table.
Findings.Headline: Customer create logs email and IBAN

Findings.Comment: The new `/orders/{id}/lines` handler injects `JdbcTemplate` into `OrderController` and runs `queryForList(...)` directly from the controller, bypassing `OrderService` entirely. This breaks the project rule that controllers never access the database and that every query goes through a service; the query itself also leaks table shape (`order_lines`, `sku`, `qty`) into the web layer. Move the query behind `OrderService` (e.g. a `lines(long id)` method) and have the controller delegate, as the sibling `get(...)` handler already does via `orders.find(id)`.
Findings.Headline: New order-lines endpoint queries the database directly from the controller
Evidence: return jdbc.queryForList("SELECT sku, qty FROM order_lines WHERE order_id = ?", id);

Expected.why: The new endpoint queries order_lines from the controller, which the blocking rule forbids. A reviewer may anchor on the query (29), the method (28) or the injected field (15).

Findings.Comment: The new `Get` handler loads an invoice by id via `h.Store.Invoice(r.Context(), r.PathValue("id"))` and returns it without checking that the invoice belongs to the caller's tenant. Any authenticated caller who can guess or obtain an invoice id from another tenant receives that tenant's invoice data. Project guidelines require `authz.SameTenant(r, inv.TenantID)` before returning an invoice loaded by id; the `List` handler right above it scopes by `authz.Tenant(r)`, so `Get` is the one path bypassing tenancy.
Findings.Headline: Invoice Get handler skips the tenant ownership check

Expected.why: Get returns any invoice by id to any caller; the blocking rule demands authz.SameTenant first. Anchors anywhere from the signature (25) to the encode (31) are honest.

Findings.Comment: The end clamp was removed, so `items[start : start+size]` runs with an upper bound that can exceed `len(items)`. The guard above only checks `start >= len(items)`, so any page that starts inside the slice but runs past its end panics with a slice-bounds error: with 5 items and `size` 3, page 2 gives `start = 3`, `start+size = 6`, and `items[3:6]` panics. Any caller paging until it sees an empty page hits this on the last partial page.
Findings.Headline: page() panics on the last partial page without an end clamp

Expected.why: Without the clamp, start+size passes len(items) on a partial last page and the slice expression panics. No blocking rule covers it.

Findings.Comment: `Deliver` now returns as soon as `retryable(lastErr)` is true, and only falls through to the log/backoff/retry path when it is false. `retryable` reports `!errors.Is(err, ErrPermanent)`, i.e. true for transient failures, so the retry policy is inverted: a subscriber answering 503 yields a transient error from `post`, `retryable` returns true, and the notification is dropped after a single attempt, while a 404 (wrapped in `ErrPermanent`) is re-sent five times and logged "will retry". This contradicts the contract documented directly above `Deliver` ("A transient failure is retried with exponential backoff, a permanent one is returned at once") and makes `baseBackoff`/`maxBackoff`/`maxAttempts` apply only to deliveries that can never succeed.
Findings.Headline: Retry condition inverted: transient errors return, permanent ones retry

Expected.why: Transient failures such as a 503 are now returned on the first attempt without any retry, while permanently rejected deliveries are retried five times with backoff.

Findings.Comment: `FetchDiff` now builds and executes its request with `context.Background()` instead of the caller's `ctx`, so the caller's cancellation and deadline are ignored even though the function's own doc comment promises "The caller's context bounds the whole operation, including the body read." Realistic scenario: a caller with a 5s timeout hits a slow or stalled Bitbucket instance — the HTTP round trip and the capped body read in `getTextCapped(context.Background(), req, maxDiffBytes)` keep running past the deadline, hanging the request goroutine and leaking the connection instead of aborting. The same `ctx` also needs to be restored in the `getTextCapped` call on the last line.
Findings.Headline: FetchDiff ignores the caller context and cannot be cancelled
Findings.Suggestion: req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u, nil)
Evidence: // The caller's context bounds the whole operation, including the body read.

Expected.why: ctx is a parameter but never used; context.Background() is passed to both NewRequestWithContext and getTextCapped, so the caller's timeout and cancellation cannot stop the request or the body read. Bitbucket has no Client.Timeout by design, which makes the caller's ctx the only bound on a 10 MiB diff.

Findings.Comment: `Store.Touch` now takes a TTL in milliseconds (`ttlMillis` is forwarded to `PExpire`), but `Hold` still converts `d` with `d.Seconds()`. A caller asking to hold a session for 5 minutes gets a Redis TTL of 300 milliseconds, so the session expires during the export instead of staying alive; any hold shorter than one second truncates to `0` and is rejected as a non-positive TTL. This defeats the whole purpose of `Hold` for the long-running export it is documented for.
Findings.Headline: Hold passes seconds to a TTL parameter now in milliseconds
Evidence: // Touch resets the remaining lifetime of session id to ttlMillis
// milliseconds. It returns ErrNotFound when the session no longer exists.
func (s *Store) Touch(ctx context.Context, id string, ttlMillis int64) error {

Expected.why: Touch now takes milliseconds, so a hold of two hours sets a lifetime of 7.2 seconds and the session expires while the export it was meant to cover is still running.

Findings.Comment: This block adds a plaintext credential for the reporting database directly into the application's main configuration. `application.yaml` is packaged into the artifact and typically committed to the repo, so the password is exposed to anyone with repository or image access and will remain in history even after it is rotated. The primary `spring.datasource` block above resolves its values from `INVENTORY_DB_*` environment variables, so this bypasses the secret-handling pattern the file already follows. Rotate the credential and load it at runtime the same way.
Findings.Headline: Hardcoded reporting database password committed in application.yaml

Expected.why: The reporting replica's password is committed in the application config, readable by everyone with repository access, while the existing datasource takes its password from the environment.

Findings.Comment: The diff adds a hardcoded credential literal `"admin123"` as the password for the reporting pool, and hardcodes the reporting URL and user alongside it — directly contradicting the class javadoc which states credentials come from the environment at deploy time. The `inventory` pool in the same class correctly uses `@Value("${INVENTORY_DB_PASSWORD}")`; the reporting pool should follow the same pattern.
Findings.Headline: Hardcoded reporting DB password committed in DataSourceConfig

Findings.Comment: `Delete` reads and mutates `c.items` while `Set` and `Get` guard the same map with `c.mu`. On a cache shared between goroutines — the design the mutex exists for — a caller that expires a key while another goroutine stores or reads one gets an unsynchronized concurrent map write/read, which in Go is a fatal `concurrent map writes` crash, not merely a stale result. Every other method on this type takes the lock; `Delete` needs it too.
Findings.Headline: Cache.Delete mutates the map without holding the mutex
Findings.Suggestion:
func (c *Cache) Delete(key string) bool {
	c.mu.Lock()
	defer c.mu.Unlock()
	_, ok := c.items[key]
	delete(c.items, key)
	return ok
}

Expected.why: Delete touches c.items without c.mu while Set and Get hold it: a data race, and Go aborts the process on a concurrent map write.

Findings.Comment: `sourceAccountId` and `requesterAccountId` are both `Long`, so `!=` compares object identity, not the wrapped value. Java caches boxed `Long` values only in the range -128..127; for any account id outside that range the two boxes are distinct objects even when the ids are equal, and the owner's own cancellation is rejected with `TransferAccessDeniedException`. On a realistic dataset where account ids run past 127, every such cancel fails while small-id accounts work, which points at data rather than the comparison.
Findings.Headline: Cancel authorization compares Long ids with != by identity

Expected.why: Boxed Longs are compared by reference, so for any account id above 127 the owner's own cancellation is rejected as access denied.

Findings.Comment: Replacing `defer r.mu.Unlock()` with an explicit `r.mu.Unlock()` at the tail leaves the early return on line 20 holding the lock: calling `Disable` with an unregistered slug takes `r.mu.Lock()` and then returns `fmt.Errorf(...)` before reaching the unlock. Any subsequent call that acquires `r.mu` (another `Disable`, or anything else on `Registry`) blocks forever, so a single typo'd or stale slug wedges the whole registry.
Findings.Headline: Disable leaks the registry lock on the unknown-slug path

Expected.why: The Unlock now runs only on the success path, so returning the unknown-team error leaves r.mu locked and every subsequent caller blocks forever.

Findings.Comment: `Summarize` documents that a ticket is optional and the guard for `r.Ticket == nil` still exists, but this change replaced its `return r.Body` with a comment, so execution falls straight through to `r.Ticket.Key`. Any caller passing a `Result` with a nil `Ticket` — the exact case the guard exists for and the comment says is allowed — now panics with a nil pointer dereference instead of returning the body.
Findings.Headline: Nil `Ticket` guard no longer returns, causing a nil deref
Evidence: // Ticket is optional; fall through to the shared renderer.

Expected.why: The nil branch no longer returns, so r.Ticket.Key panics whenever Ticket is nil. A reviewer may anchor on the dead check (19) or on the dereference (22).

Findings.Comment: Setting `last` to `len(lines) + 1` makes the subsequent `lines[first:last]` slice one element past the end of the slice. Any input where the requested trailing context reaches or passes the end of the file hits this: e.g. 20 lines, `n = 5`, and a hunk with `first = 17` gives `last = 22`, the clamp sets `last = 21`, and `lines[17:21]` panics with "slice bounds out of range". It also contradicts the stated contract that the window must stop at the last line of the file — the last line is index `len(lines)-1`, already covered by `last = len(lines)`.
Findings.Headline: ContextAfter clamps past end of slice and panics on EOF context

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: `WhoAmI` calls `c.http.Do(req)` and then, on every path — the non-2xx error return, the `json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode` failure, and the success return — hands back without ever closing `resp.Body`, since the `defer resp.Body.Close()` that used to guard it was deleted. Each call therefore leaks the underlying TCP connection and its file descriptor: a caller polling `WhoAmI` (e.g. validating tokens on a request path) will accumulate unclosed bodies until the process runs out of descriptors or stops reusing connections.
Findings.Headline: WhoAmI never closes the HTTP response body

Expected.why: The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Findings.Comment: `worker` now writes `q.depth = len(q.pending)` with no lock held, while `Depth()` reads the same field under `q.mu`. Any caller invoking `Depth()` while a job finishes — e.g. a status endpoint polling the backlog while the single review completes — performs an unsynchronized read/write on the same `int`, which is a data race in Go: the race detector flags it and the read value is undefined. The lock was the only thing serializing these accesses, so removing it breaks the invariant the `Depth()` path still relies on.
Findings.Headline: Depth counter written without holding the mutex

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: `getRates` wraps `return this.refresh(base)` in try/catch without awaiting the returned promise. Because `refresh` is async, a rejection from `provider.fetch` (or `cache.set`) rejects the promise handed to the caller and never enters this `catch`, so the new stale-serving path is unreachable: the moment the provider starts failing, every request with an expired cached table throws instead of falling back to the cached rates — exactly the case this change is meant to cover.
Findings.Headline: Provider-failure fallback never runs: refresh() is not awaited in try/catch

Expected.why: The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: The commit's error is now discarded, so a failed `COMMIT` (connection drop, serialization failure, constraint violation deferred to commit, context cancellation) is reported to the caller as success. A caller retrying or acknowledging the claim would then believe the team's claim was persisted when no row exists.
Findings.Headline: AddClaim silently ignores the transaction commit error

Findings.Comment: `Owner` now wraps the two error cases the wrong way round: a missing claim returns the raw driver error (`errNoRows`), while an actual database fault is wrapped as `ErrNoClaim`. Any caller that decides "unclaimed project" versus "database failure" with `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` — the distinction the doc comment above promises — will treat a connection failure or SQL error as "nobody owns this project" and will not recognize a genuinely unclaimed project at all. On realistic input (project key absent from `team_claims`, or a transient DB outage) the error classification is exactly inverted, which can lead to silent misattribution of ownership or lost error handling.
Findings.Headline: Owner wraps no-rows and database errors in the wrong sentinel

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
